title: Write a short text, then improve it
intro: I can write for a reader and reread to make my meaning clearer.
exampleTitle: An edit should help the reader
example: Draft: “my bird have wing”. Revised report: “My bird has wings.” My needs a capital at the beginning; has fits one bird; wings names the parts; the full stop closes the statement. A report shares checkable information. An opinion such as “I like birds because I enjoy their songs” gives a view and a reason.
steps: 1. Choose your message
Decide who will read and what you want to share: facts, an opinion or events. Say each simple sentence before writing it. Use helpful topic words.
Facts supplied: a pencil has a point; it makes marks. A recount instead tells ordered actions: “I drew a star. Then I coloured it.”
Write two report sentences about the supplied pencil facts.

For example: “A pencil has a point. It makes marks.” Accept other accurate simple sentences. For a different purpose, write a preference with a relevant reason or connected events in order; do not label every text a report.
2. Connect pictures and words
Make a drawing and caption about the same action. A short sequence needs pictures and captions in a sensible order.
Paper model: draw a hand folding paper, then a hand drawing a star on the folded card. Captions: “First, I fold the paper.” “Then I draw a star.”
Make two different pictures about packing a bag and add matching captions.

Look for a clear sequence and captions that match the actual learner drawings. Accept different relevant actions. An adult can help create, order and caption images on a device; paper work alone does not demonstrate digital creation.
3. Reread, change and check
Check meaning and complete sentences first. Add a useful word or remove an unnecessary one. Check capitals, end marks and uncertain spellings against a reliable reference.
Draft: “i saw a rabit rabit”. Reference spelling: rabbit. Revision: “I saw a rabbit.” Capital I, correct spelling, remove repetition, full stop.
Edit “the dog run run”. Keep a statement about one dog.
“The dog runs.” Capitalise The, use runs for one dog, remove the repeated run and add a full stop. Accept a relevant addition such as “The dog runs fast.” Explain why each change helps.
mistakes: “Longer is always better.”
Choose details that help the meaning.
“Every word needs a capital.”
Use a capital for the beginning and proper names, not every word.
“Guess every spelling.”
Notice an uncertain word and use a word wall or dictionary.
activity: Write a short report from the pencil facts, an opinion about a familiar activity, or a real or imagined two-event recount. Draw a matching picture. Read your text to a partner and make one useful change, or explain why a checked sentence is already clear.
adjust: Starter: say a sentence with an adult and use a word bank. Core: write and reread your own short text. Stretch: improve a detail and explain your edit without making the text unnecessarily long.
safety: Observe the actual written or multimodal text and note any scribing or prompts. A scribe can support ideas but does not show the child’s spelling or handwriting.
tricky: 1. Is “I like this game” a report fact?
It states an opinion. A reason can explain the preference.
2. Must an edit add words?
No. Removing repetition or correcting a word can improve meaning.
3. Does a picture prove its character’s name?
No. Supply a name explicitly if needed; do not infer invisible facts.
faq: Must every text be long?
No. Short connected sentences can show the skill.
Which end mark should I use?
A statement usually ends with a full stop; a question needs a question mark. Choose an exclamation mark for a fitting exclamation or urgent warning.
modelCaption: Read the whole sentence after each edit

title: Plan and give a clear short talk
intro: I can organise a short presentation and help a listener follow it.
exampleTitle: Three parts keep one topic clear
example: “Our group made a paper fan. We folded the paper back and forth. The folds help it open and close. Our fan is ready to use.” The first sentence opens the topic, the middle explains useful details, and the last finishes it. In an actual talk, show your fan and point to a fold as you name it.
steps: 1. Plan a beginning, middle and ending
Name your topic, choose connected details and finish with a final thought. Small word or picture cues help you remember without reading a long script.
Model: “This is my water bottle. The lid closes the top. I carry it to school. My bottle keeps my drink together.”
Plan a short talk about a familiar object and give it to a listener.
Observe a named topic, relevant middle and connected conclusion. Accept varied accurate details. A polite thank you can follow the final thought, but does not replace it.
2. Fit details to the purpose
A report tells what happened; an explanation gives ordered actions; a recommendation gives a choice and reason. Explain useful topic words.
Group record: “We sorted buttons into small and large groups.” Report the size grouping. To explain how, say “Look at each button. Put small ones together and large ones together.”
Recommend this game with a reason: one player claps a pattern, others copy, then the next player leads.

For example: “We should try this game because everyone gets a turn to lead.” Accept another reason supported by the rules. The child communicates a real recommendation, not just selects a printed model.
3. Rehearse for your listener
Use a comfortable audible voice, a followable pace and helpful pauses. A gesture or picture should add meaning. Ask what was hard to hear or follow, then adjust.
Adult says “Draw a circle. Put a dot inside it.” once rushed, then with a pause after each instruction. A partner follows the actual spoken directions.
Give different two-step directions. Pause so your partner can act, then ask what helped.

Observe whether the listener can hear and follow the message. Repair unclear words as well as pace. For another purpose, try the original rhyme “A little boat. A little float.” with a flowing rhythm and useful pause; speak both versions to compare.
mistakes: “Louder is always clearer.”
Match volume to the room and listener; do not shout.
“A picture is enough by itself.”
Explain and refer to its useful feature.
“Eye contact proves a good talk.”
Listen for understandable content and delivery; do not grade gaze or accent.
activityTitle: Plan, present and improve one part
activity: Choose an interest or something you made. Plan opening, two details and final thought. Show a real object or learner drawing and point to a useful part. Present to a partner, ask about volume and pace, rehearse a helpful change, then present again.
adjust: Starter: use three adult-supported cues. Core: give the connected talk with relevant topic words. Stretch: change the purpose or audience and explain which details or delivery need changing.
safety: Observe actual delivery and record prompts. Seated presentation, signing, AAC and other supports can aid participation; record any speech-specific feature that was not observed. Confidence is not a score.
tricky: 1. Can a conclusion introduce a new unrelated topic?
That makes the ending harder to follow. Finish the current topic.
2. Does “because I like it” explain a game’s benefit?
It states liking. Add a useful feature or explain what you enjoy.
3. Can a pause help?
Yes. A pause between ideas can let the listener understand or act.
faq: Does the child need to memorise every word?
No. Brief cues can support an understandable talk.
Can a written plan show suitable volume?
No. Listen to the actual presentation to judge audibility and pace.
modelCaption: One connected topic across three parts
modelCards: Middle: The folds help it open.
Conclusion: It is ready to use.

title: Write clear, unjoined words
intro: I can write lower-case and capital letters in words with comfortable control.
example: Use the actual handwriting models in More examples and your school’s taught forms. In bag, b is tall, a stays small and g has a tail below the baseline. An adult models each start and movement. Copy the word on suitable lines, lift the pencil between letters and read it back. A typed word is a spelling cue, not a stroke-direction model.
steps: 1. Get ready for controlled movement
Sit comfortably, support your arm and steady the paper with your other hand. Hold the pencil so you can guide it without squeezing hard.
Adult demonstrates one school-taught letter, showing its start and movement. Try the movement in the air, then on paper in a short familiar word.
Write a short word while an adult watches your hand. What helps it feel comfortable?
Observe comfortable, controlled movement and readable forms. Different functional grasps can work. Pause if the hand is sore or tired; follow individual school or specialist support.
2. Use both letter cases in words
Unjoined letters have no joining strokes. Capitals and lower-case partners can look different. Use the school’s model rather than making every small letter bigger.
The retained model shows B beside b and E beside e. The name Ava starts with capital A followed by lower-case v and a.
Watch an adult model the name Ben in the taught style. Copy it with unjoined letters.
Look for a recognisable capital B then lower-case e and n in order, with separate letter movements. Provide a model so spelling memory does not become the handwriting test.
3. Check placement and word gaps
Most letter bodies sit on the baseline; tails extend below it in the taught model. Small gaps separate letters, while a larger gap separates words.
The phrase “a red bag” has three words. Copy it on paper after an adult models it. Read the words back and compare their gaps.
Write “a red bag”. Choose one clear letter or gap, then improve one that needs help.
Observe three readable words, unjoined forms and larger word gaps. Accept school-taught letter styles. A clear first attempt need not be changed just to create an improvement.
mistakes: “Every letter is the same height.”
Compare tall letters, small bodies and tails using the taught model.
“Only one grip is allowed.”
Check comfort and functional control.
“Typing proves handwriting.”
Observe the child producing the actual pen or pencil marks.
activityTitle: Watch, copy and check a label
activity: Choose a short familiar name or object word. An adult supplies and demonstrates it in the school’s unjoined style. Copy it on lined paper to make a label. Read it back and check one shape, line placement or word gap.
adjust: Starter: use larger lines and a nearby model, tracing briefly if useful. Core: copy without tracing and check the result. Stretch: write a short phrase while keeping comfortable control and readable word gaps.
safety: Observe the hand and finished sample. Spelling knowledge, artistic quality and speed are separate. These examples begin a continuing repertoire of school-taught lower-case and capital forms.
tricky: 1. Is a capital always a bigger lower-case shape?
No. B/b and E/e illustrate different forms.
2. Must each letter join the next?
No. This code calls for unjoined letters.
3. Can a neat copied word reveal the pencil grip?
No. Watch the actual writing movement and comfort too.
faq: Which handwriting style should we use?
Use the forms and starting points taught at the child’s school; the retained examples are NSW/ACT-style models.
Can a scribe show the child’s handwriting?
A scribe supports ideas, but the child must produce the marks for handwriting evidence.
modelCaption: Use a real school model beside your writing
modelCards: Check shape, line and word gaps

title: Hear every sound in a word
intro: I can separate spoken words into sounds and keep their order, including clusters.
example: Adult says shop without showing its spelling. Say its sounds: /sh/ /o/ /p/. Move three counters. In stop, say /s/ /t/ /o/ /p/ and move four counters. The two beginning sounds in stop remain separate. The printed sh in shop represents one sound. Say the whole word again to check.
steps: 1. Listen and separate
A phoneme is one speech sound. Say a familiar word naturally, stretch where possible, then say each sound in order. Avoid adding an extra “uh” after consonants.
Adult models map: /m/ /a/ /p/, then blends back to map. Three counters stand for the three sounds.
Adult says fish with its spelling hidden. Say every sound and move one counter each.
/f/ /i/ /sh/: three sounds. Hear the actual response; the last sound is one /sh/. Counters support the oral task, not letter counting.
2. Keep the beginning cluster
A consonant cluster has adjacent consonant sounds. Listen for each one instead of treating the cluster as a single sound.
Flag: /f/ /l/ /a/ /g/. There are four sounds; /f/ and /l/ both come before the vowel.
Adult says swim without showing its spelling. Separate every sound, then blend back.
/s/ /w/ /i/ /m/: four sounds, in order. If /w/ is missed, model it and try again. Note the support rather than calling the repeated model independent.
3. Keep the ending cluster
Listen through to the end. A correct total alone is not enough: say each sound in its right place.
Nest: /n/ /e/ /s/ /t/. Both /s/ and /t/ need a counter.
Adult says lamp with spelling hidden. Say the sounds and identify the last two.
/l/ /a/ /m/ /p/: four sounds. The final two are /m/ /p/. Accept ordinary accent variation; do not substitute syllable claps for the phoneme response.
mistakes: “A letter is always one sound.”
Listen first: sh can represent one sound.
“A cluster is one sound.”
Keep each consonant, as /s/ and /t/ in stop.
“The correct number is enough.”
Ask for the full ordered sound sequence, then blend back.
activity: Adult chooses a few familiar spoken words such as map, fish, flag and nest, keeping spellings hidden. Child repeats each whole word, says its sounds with one counter each, then blends back. Use fewer words if attention or effort drops.
adjust: Starter: model a three-sound word. Core: keep both sounds in beginning and ending clusters. Stretch: try stamp, /s/ /t/ /a/ /m/ /p/, keeping all five sounds in order.
safety: Use counters, large tokens or pointing as appropriate. Observe actual segmentation. Accent and speech access needs require thoughtful support; a written choice does not establish an oral response.
tricky: 1. Does shop need four sound counters?
No. /sh/ /o/ /p/ has three sounds.
2. Can you leave out the last sound of nest?
No. /t/ is part of the spoken word.
3. Is one clap for stop the same task?
No. Stop is one syllable but has four phonemes.
faq: Should I show the spelling first?
For the oral check, hide it. Afterward, letters can help connect sounds to spelling.
Must every sound be stretched?
No. Some consonants are brief stop sounds. Say them cleanly without an added vowel.
modelCaption: Listen to sounds rather than count letters

title: Change a sound to make a new word
intro: I can add, replace or remove a spoken sound while keeping the others in order.
exampleTitle: Change one position, keep the rest
example: Adult says sip with no printed target shown. Say /s/ /i/ /p/. Add /l/ immediately after /s/: /s/ /l/ /i/ /p/. Blend to say slip. You added one sound inside the word; you did not replace a sound or move the new one to the front. Use one counter per sound to show the position.
steps: 1. Add a sound
Keep every old sound and place one new sound exactly where asked. Say and blend the result. Practise one position at a time.
At + /s/ at the beginning gives sat. Ten + /t/ at the end gives tent. Sip + /l/ after /s/ gives slip. These have at most four sounds.
Adult says ram. Add /p/ at the end and say the new word.
Ramp: /r/ /a/ /m/ /p/. All the original sounds stay in order. Ask for the spoken word before revealing its spelling.
2. Replace one sound
Substitute means take one sound out and put a different sound in the same position. Leave the other sounds alone.
Change /m/ in mat to /s/: sat. Change the middle vowel in pin to the vowel in pen: pen. Change final /t/ in pet to /g/: peg.
Adult says cap. Replace its last sound with /t/ and say the new word.
Cat. /k/ and the short vowel stay; /p/ changes to /t/. Hear the child make the change rather than copy a displayed answer.
3. Remove one sound
Delete means take away the stated sound without adding a replacement. Touch the remaining counters and blend their sounds.
Remove first /s/ from stop: top. Remove /l/ from clap: cap. Remove final /t/ from tent: ten.
Adult says sand. Remove /n/, the sound just before the final /d/. What word remains?
Sad: /s/ /a/ /d/. Keep the final /d/. If needed, show four counters, remove the third and blend the others; record this support.
mistakes: “Add means replace.”
Adding keeps the original sounds and creates one more position.
“Any sound can disappear.”
Remove only the sound named.
“A silent written swap proves the skill.”
Listen to the actual new spoken word.
activityTitle: One change in a short spoken word
activity: With printed spellings hidden, adult gives one instruction at a time: add /s/ before top; replace /m/ in mat with /s/; remove /l/ from clap. Check the spoken results stop, sat and cap afterward. Ask the child to show which counter changed.
adjust: Starter: model and guide one operation. Core: produce new words for clear beginning, middle and end changes. Stretch: explain a change between two familiar one-syllable words with no more than four sounds.
safety: The displayed words guide the adult. Keep them out of the learner’s view for oral checks. Use short clean sounds, familiar vocabulary and ordinary accent variation; do not confuse letters with phonemes.
tricky: 1. Is deleting /k/ from clap the same as deleting /l/?
No. Removing /k/ gives lap; removing /l/ gives cap. Position matters.
2. Can one sound use two written letters?
Yes. /sh/ is one sound in ship; a sound change need not be one letter change.
3. If cap becomes clap, did /k/ disappear?
No. /l/ was added after /k/; the original sounds remain.
faq: Should we teach every operation in one sitting?
No. Model one operation and position, give supported turns, then combine familiar changes when ready.
Do counters replace speaking?
They show sound positions. Observe the actual new spoken word for this oral skill, and note communication support.
modelCaption: Add, replace and remove have different jobs

title: Use sounds and spelling patterns to read and write
intro: I can blend and write short words and familiar two-syllable words.
exampleTitle: A digraph and a cluster work differently
example: Ship has /sh/ /i/ /p/: sh represents one sound. Slip has /s/ /l/ /i/ /p/: s and l represent separate sounds. Read through the complete word. For spelling, hear a word with the printed model hidden, say the sounds, choose taught letters or patterns, write it and read it back.
steps: 1. Notice the vowel pattern
Learn short vowels and common long-vowel spellings through familiar words. A long vowel often sounds like its letter name. Read the whole word; no one pattern works in every word.
Cap has a short vowel. Cape has a long a sound in the a–consonant–e pattern. Rain and day show two other common long a spellings.
Read kit and kite aloud. What written part helps you distinguish them?
Kit has short i; kite has long i and includes final e in the pattern. Hear independent reading before an adult supplies the words. Do not infer a separate syllable for final e.
2. Keep blends and digraphs clear
In a blend, keep each consonant sound. A digraph uses two letters for one sound. Say the whole word to check rather than guess from the first letter.
Wish: /w/ /i/ /sh/. Rest: /r/ /e/ /s/ /t/. Both have short vowels; only rest ends with two separate consonant sounds.
Read chin and clap. Then cover them and write one, saying its sounds.
Chin begins with the single /ch/ sound; clap begins /k/ /l/. Check the chosen standard spelling after writing. If the adult dictated it first, record spelling rather than independent reading.
3. Join familiar syllables
A two-syllable word has two spoken parts, each with a vowel sound. Blend within each part and join them into the whole word. Use meaning to check, not to guess.
Sunset: sun–set. Bedtime: bed–time, with short e then long i. Read both parts before joining.
Read napkin aloud. Cover it, write it and read your writing back.
Nap–kin joins to napkin. Check n-a-p-k-i-n, both vowel letters and the order. Copying a visible word is useful practice but does not show spelling without the model.
mistakes: “A blend is a single sound.”
Keep both sounds in /k/ /l/.
“Every final e makes a long vowel.”
Learn common patterns and word-specific exceptions such as have.
“The first letter is enough.”
Read all the sounds and syllables.
activity: Choose a few taught words from wish, rest, rain, kite, sunset and bedtime. Child reads each before an adult says it. Then hide the model, dictate a chosen word, write it and compare with the spelling. Note reading and writing separately.
adjust: Starter: model one familiar short-vowel word. Core: read and write digraph, blend and common long-vowel words. Stretch: combine familiar patterns in a two-syllable word, such as raincoat, after teaching both parts.
safety: Use the child’s taught phonics sequence and ordinary accent. The printed targets must be visible for reading and hidden during the spelling attempt. Extra reading support is recorded, not treated as independent decoding.
tricky: 1. Can ship be a short-vowel word and a digraph word?
Yes. The vowel and consonant spelling describe different features.
2. Does kite have two syllables because it has i and e?
No. It has one spoken vowel sound and one syllable.
3. Is reading a word after the adult says it independent decoding?
It may be supported practice. Check independent reading before supplying the target.
faq: Do we need to learn every spelling pattern at once?
No. Practise taught correspondences, then add useful new ones gradually.
Why read the written word back?
It helps notice missing sounds, wrong order or a spelling that changes the word; compare with the standard spelling too.

title: Compare letter sounds and hear syllables
intro: I can notice different letter–sound links and hear the vowel sound in each syllable.
exampleTitle: Count spoken parts, not written vowels
example: Rain has two vowel letters, ai, representing one vowel sound here: one syllable. Sunset has two spoken parts, sun and set, each with a vowel sound: two syllables. Listen to the word naturally before marking its parts. The model shows these particular words, not a rule that every vowel pair makes one sound.
steps: 1. One letter can represent different sounds
Compare the actual sounds in familiar words. The same letter does not always represent the same sound.
Listen to adult models cut, put and use. The letter u represents different vowel sounds in these words. Also compare a in cat, father and any.
Hear cat and any. Does their written a represent the same vowel sound?

No in usual Australian pronunciation: cat has short a; any begins with a vowel like short e. Accept local accent variation and model the intended words. Do not change their spellings to match a guessed rule.
2. One sound can use different letters
A sound can be represented by different letters or groups. Look at the complete word and use what you have learned about that word.
Sat and cent both begin with the /s/ sound in usual pronunciation, written s and c. Go and gem use g for different initial sounds.
Read or hear sat and cent, then point to the letter for their shared beginning sound.
S in sat and c in cent both represent /s/. Identify the actual letter in each word; do not claim c always has that sound.
3. Hear the vowel sound in each syllable
A syllable is a spoken part containing a vowel sound. Say the whole word, then tap its parts. Each part must still fit the word you heard.
Sun: one spoken part. Robot: ro–bot, two. Cake: one, despite two written vowel letters.
Say raincoat naturally, then tap its parts. What vowel sounds can you hear?
Rain–coat: two parts, with long a in rain and long o in coat. Four written vowel letters do not make four syllables. Use familiar pronunciation rather than adding spoken sounds for silent letters.
mistakes: “A letter has only one sound.”
Compare its use in different actual words.
“Count every written vowel to count syllables.”
Listen for vowel sounds in spoken parts.
“Every vowel pair works alike.”
Check the particular word and taught pattern.
activity: Adult models cat/any, cut/put/use and sat/cent. Discuss which sound–letter link changes. Then child says sun, cake, robot and raincoat, tapping their spoken parts and hearing a vowel sound in each.
adjust: Starter: compare two adult-modelled words. Core: explain a sound–letter difference and tap one- and two-syllable words. Stretch: explain why rain and raincoat need different syllable counts.
safety: Adult models support listening; they are not independent reading evidence. Accept ordinary accent variation. Choose clear familiar words instead of forcing a pronunciation to fit the printed letters.
tricky: 1. Does rain have two syllables?
No. In usual pronunciation it has one vowel sound and one syllable.
2. Does c always represent /s/?
No. Compare cent with cat.
3. Can a spoken syllable have no vowel sound?
For these taught Year 1 words, listen for the vowel sound that gives each syllable its spoken beat. Avoid treating silent written letters as spoken syllables.
faq: Must the child use technical sound symbols?
No. Saying and comparing the sounds is enough; an adult can explain the terms.
Is a clap the same as a phoneme counter?
No. A clap here represents a syllable; a sound counter represents one phoneme.
modelCaption: Written vowel letters and spoken syllables can differ
modelCards: Each taught syllable has a vowel sound

title: Spell words using familiar patterns
intro: I can say, write and check one- and two-syllable words with common spellings.
exampleTitle: Use sounds, parts and a spelling check
example: Adult dictates sunset with the model hidden. Say sun–set. Spell the first familiar part s-u-n, then s-e-t. Join them: sunset. Read it back and compare with the standard spelling. Both parts matter; sounding out helps, while remembered and taught spelling patterns tell us which letters to choose.
steps: 1. Map sounds to taught letters
Say the word, listen in order and choose known spellings. Keep both consonants in a blend and all letters of a digraph.
Ship uses sh for its first sound. Flag needs both f and l before a and g. Nest needs both s and t at the end.
Adult hides the screen and dictates clap. Write the whole word, then check it.
Clap: c-l-a-p. Keep /k/ and /l/ at the start. A spoken segmentation supports spelling, but the child must produce the written word.
2. Write both syllables
Say each part and spell it with taught patterns. Some standard spellings include letters you cannot infer from a syllable count alone.
Napkin: nap–kin, n-a-p-k-i-n. Rabbit: two spoken parts; its taught standard spelling is r-a-b-b-i-t. Notice bb explicitly.
Adult dictates sandpit with the spelling hidden. Write and check both parts.
Sand–pit: s-a-n-d-p-i-t. Retain the final d of sand and the first p of pit. Compare only after the child attempts the spelling.
3. Check the pattern and the whole word
Read your spelling back and compare with a reliable model after trying. Locate the exact difference and rewrite the full word. A correct sound can have several spellings.
Draft: “picnik”. Reference: picnic. Compare the last letters: this word ends with c, not k. Correct the whole word and read it again.
Compare draft “rabit” with reference rabbit. What must change?
Add the second b: rabbit. Hearing two syllables does not itself prove doubling. Learn and check the standard spelling in a useful word.
mistakes: “Every sound uses one letter.”
Sh in ship represents one sound with two letters.
“Two syllables tell you every letter.”
Use taught word spellings as well as spoken parts.
“Copying is a spelling-memory check.”
Copying practises letter order; hide the model for a spelling attempt.
activity: Adult chooses a few taught words such as flag, rain, napkin and sandpit, then hides the displayed spellings. Dictate each in a short meaningful sentence. Child says its parts, writes it, reads it back and compares with a model afterward.
adjust: Starter: use a taught sound or pattern card. Core: spell one- and two-syllable targets without copying. Stretch: explain one correction or apply familiar parts in bedtime or raincoat after those spellings are taught.
safety: Keep dictation targets and answer models away from the learner during attempts. Record prompts and any reference used. A typed response can show spelling; assess handwriting separately.
tricky: 1. Can sounding out choose between every spelling of /k/?
No. Common patterns and known standard word spellings help choose c, k or ck.
2. Is a missing second part acceptable in sunset?
No. Both sun and set belong in the whole word.
3. Must a correct first attempt be changed?
No. Check it and explain what is already correct.
faq: Should every word be unfamiliar?
No. Rehearse useful taught words and add new words supported by familiar patterns.
Why use a sentence in dictation?
It identifies the intended word and meaning, especially when words can sound alike.
modelCaption: Keep the sounds, patterns and both parts

title: Read and write familiar words accurately
intro: I can build a growing set of high-frequency words and use them in meaningful text.
exampleTitle: Notice the usual and unusual parts
example: In said, s and d represent familiar sounds; ai represents the short e sound in this word. Read said, use it in “Mia said hello”, cover it, write it and check s-a-i-d. This teaches the complete spelling instead of guessing from the word’s outline. Practise a manageable set and revisit it over time.
steps: 1. Learn the whole word
Say the target, match familiar sounds to letters and notice any unusual part. High-frequency means a word occurs often; it does not mean every word follows an easy spelling rule.
Have is h-a-v-e with a short a in usual pronunciation. One is the number word o-n-e. Pretty is p-r-e-t-t-y, with its first vowel sounding like short i.
Read have, one and pretty aloud before an adult supplies the words. Which letters need attention?
Observe actual reading. Check the final e in have, the complete unusual spelling of one and the e/tt/y in pretty. Support and reteach only the parts that need it; do not demand a timed response.
2. Read it in a complete message
Read through the written word and sentence. Context helps check meaning but should not replace attention to the letters.
“I found one shell.” One means a quantity here; won names winning in another sentence. They can sound alike while having different spellings.
Read “I have some paper.” Point to and read have and some again.
Hear accurate reading of both words. Their final e does not give the common long-vowel pattern here. If the adult pre-reads the targets, record supported practice rather than independent reading.
3. Write, uncover and check
After studying a word, cover it and write it. Compare every letter, correct a mismatch, then use it in a short sentence. Later, try without a recent visible model.
Look at they. Cover it, write it and check t-h-e-y. “They can play” uses it meaningfully.
Study said, cover it, write it and check. Use it in your own short sentence.
Look for s-a-i-d and a sensible use such as “Dad said hello.” Accept different complete sentences. Retrieval after study is supported rehearsal; later unseen checks show what has been retained.
mistakes: “Remember only the word’s shape.”
Link sounds and the complete spelling, including unusual parts.
“Guess from a picture or first letter.”
Read all the letters and check the message.
“Fast is the first goal.”
Build accurate reading, then increasingly smooth recognition with practice.
activity: Choose a few needed words such as have, said and one. Read, discuss their spellings, cover and write them, then use them in a short message. Return to the collection later and add words when earlier ones are secure.
adjust: Starter: practise one adult-modelled word. Core: read and write a small taught set accurately. Stretch: use the words in a fresh sentence and retrieve their spellings on a later day.
safety: Record reading and writing separately, with prompts and dates. A few correct words do not certify a complete repertoire. Do not use speed, accent or a single recent copy as mastery evidence.
tricky: 1. Does high-frequency always mean regularly spelt?
No. Some common words include unusual sound–letter links.
2. Can one and won be swapped in “one shell”?
No. One is the number word for this meaning.
3. Must every learner find some equally difficult?
No. Choose practice from the child’s actual reading and writing evidence.
faq: Is there one fixed word list for this lesson?
No. The examples begin a growing useful repertoire; use taught words needed in reading and writing.
Is cover-write-check enough to claim independent spelling over time?
It rehearses retrieval after study. Revisit without a recent model to check retention.
modelCaption: Map the complete spelling, then use it

title: Build word families from meaningful parts
intro: I can find a base word and use endings to change how it works in a sentence.
exampleTitle: A shared base carries shared meaning
example: Play, plays, played and playing retain the meaningful base play. “I played yesterday” uses ed for a past action. “I am playing now” uses am with playing for the ongoing action now. “I was playing yesterday” shows that ing alone does not always mean now. Check the whole sentence.
steps: 1. Find a meaningful base
A base carries the central meaning. Endings can change number or how a verb fits its sentence. Similar rhyme or starting letters do not prove a family.
Help, helps, helped and helping share help. Yelp may sound similar but does not contain that meaningful base.
Find the base in jumping and jumped. Does bump belong to this same base family?
Jump is the shared base. Bump rhymes but has a different base and meaning. Read both complete family words, not just the shared letters.
2. Let the sentence guide the ending
Noun s can show more than one; verb s can fit a singular subject. Ed often marks a regular past form. Ing works with other words to express an ongoing action.
“The cats run” has plural cats. “The cat runs” uses runs for one cat. “We walked yesterday” uses walked for the past.
Complete “The dog is ___ now” using bark. Then complete “The dog ___ yesterday.”
Barking fits the first sentence; barked fits the second. Accept the complete forms in their sentences. Do not treat every s as plural or every ing word as present time.
3. Read and build the family
Find the base, notice an ending and blend the whole word. Some endings sound different across words, and some spellings change. Learn useful examples without inventing an always-rule.
Look + ed gives looked. Play + ed gives played. Ed is not always an extra spoken syllable. Playground joins meaningful play and ground; it is a related compound, not a grammatical ending.
Build three forms from wash and use one in a sentence.

Washes, washed and washing are useful forms. For example, “I washed my hands yesterday.” Accept another grammatical sentence. Explain the base wash and the ending used; teach any unfamiliar ending spelling.
mistakes: “Word families are just rhymes.”
Look for a shared meaningful base.
“Every s means many.”
Compare noun cats with verb runs.
“Ing always means now.”
Compare am playing now with was playing yesterday.
activityTitle: Build, read and use a family
activity: Write help on a card and s, ed and ing on separate cards. Build helps, helped and helping, read each complete word and use it in a sentence. Compare “She helps each day”, “She helped yesterday” and “She is helping now”. Then try a different familiar base.
adjust: Starter: identify the shared base with an adult. Core: build endings and use them in complete sentences. Stretch: compare a plural noun with a singular verb ending, or notice a familiar compound such as playground.
safety: Assess meaning and use, not only colour matching or card placement. Observe actual reading when checking reading. Spelling changes such as clapped/clapping need explicit teaching; do not teach “just add” as a universal rule.
tricky: 1. Do look and book form this kind of word family?
No. They rhyme but do not share the same meaningful base.
2. Does runs mean more than one runner?
No. In “The cat runs”, s makes the verb fit one cat.
3. Does walked need a separate ed syllable?
Not in usual pronunciation. Recognise walk and ed, then read the whole word naturally.
faq: Can related words use more than an ending?
Yes. Playground combines play and ground; distinguish a compound from grammatical endings.
Must we teach every spelling change at once?
No. Begin with familiar regular families and explicitly teach useful changes as needed.
modelCaption: Check the base, ending and complete sentence
modelCards: The cats run. / The cat runs.
am playing now / was playing yesterday
